messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele was a 66-year-old divorced woman of Pacific Islander background who had run the same neighborhood shop for years, a small place where she knew regular customers by name and had once taken pride in being steady under pressure. The event that brought her to treatment happened in her store late in the afternoon, near closing, at the same hour she still now dreaded each day. A police officer had come in after some confusion outside and, within minutes, the encounter turned violent. What stayed with her most clearly was not a coherent sequence but flashes: the officer’s stare fixed on her as if she were dangerous, the sensation of the room tipping, her body going light and unsteady, and the humiliation of being handled with force in her own shop while watched. She could not give a full account of what happened between those moments. When she tried, whole stretches were simply absent, and even the fragments she did have felt so extreme that she sometimes said it was hard to believe it had happened to her. Often she would stop speaking altogether and press a hand to her chest or temple, saying there were no words for it.

In the weeks afterward, late afternoon became charged. As the light shifted toward the hour of the assault, Mele would feel dizzy in the shop and abruptly aware of windows, mirrors, and anyone lingering near the counter. If a customer stood back and seemed to watch her, or if she caught sight of someone outside looking in, her mind would snag on the event without yielding a clear story. In those moments, the reminder did not stop at fear; it brought with it the judgment that this was what she had become, a woman who could not even stand in her own store without coming apart. A customer’s lingering glance could make her think, with immediate shame, that she was weak and no longer capable of coping. The same lightheaded feeling she had during the assault seemed to pull up those broken, unreal fragments. Because the memory arrived in pieces and without language, she came to fear what her reactions said about her. Once those fragments had been stirred, ordinary details around her took on the charge of warning signs: the slant of late-day light, a face paused at the window, the sense of someone standing back and watching. The more the memory surfaced in that disjointed way, the more widely she began to recognize pieces of it in the shop around her. She had begun telling herself that a competent woman would have been able to get over this, and that the fact she froze, lost words, and could not think straight meant she was inadequate, a lousy coper, maybe even going crazy.

Those beliefs hardened each time she tried to make sense of the assault and found only blanks. The missing parts felt intolerable to her. She took her inability to remember as proof that something was wrong with her mind, not as a consequence of terror. When she said the event felt unreal, she did not mean it was unimportant; she meant that its extremity made her doubt herself. That self-doubt seemed to push the memory even further out of reach. In session she would circle around the assault, describing the officer’s eyes, the dizziness, the sense of being pinned in place, but when she tried to connect one moment to the next she became mute and agitated, as if believing she was “going crazy” made the memory less speakable.

Over months, Mele organized her life around not being caught in that state. In the shop she began asking an employee to handle the register near closing time, or she shut the gate earlier so she would not be there at that hour. She avoided dates connected to the event and refused suggestions from family to mark them in any way. These precautions did not shrink the problem; they gave it more landmarks. The earlier she closed, the more late afternoon itself became a signal of danger, and the more the avoided dates and routines stood out in her mind as reminders of what had happened. If she had to stay late and felt the familiar dizziness or the sense of being watched, she would leave the front of the store, go into the back room, or close altogether. At home she increasingly bought things online or from wholesalers she did not need—small household goods, extra stock, decorative items—because spending gave her a brief, numbing comfort and something concrete to focus on instead of the fragments in her head. Yet these strategies narrowed her life. Customers noticed she was less available late in the day, and she felt ashamed needing help in a business she had managed alone.

The more she cut herself off from reminders, the stranger the memory became. Avoiding the hour, the dates, and the circumstances that brought the assault to mind kept her from testing whether she could bear remembering, and the event remained a set of disconnected sensations rather than a story. After impulsive purchases she would berate herself for lacking discipline, taking the spending itself as further evidence that she was not coping and was slipping mentally. She also became more sensitive to the triggers she was trying to outrun: by midafternoon she scanned for who might be looking at her, noticed every spell of lightheadedness, and braced for the familiar sense that something terrible was about to break through. Those moments made the memory feel nearer and less graspable at once.

By the time Mele sought help, the pattern had tightened around both her work and her sense of herself. What finally brought her in was a recent late-afternoon episode in the shop when a man stood silently near the doorway and she became so dizzy and frightened that she locked up early, then spent hundreds of dollars online that night trying to settle down. She arrived embarrassed and wary, convinced that her reactions meant she was failing in some fundamental way. What frightened her most was not only the memory of the officer’s violence, but the possibility that if she stopped avoiding it she would lose her mind completely; what she hoped, cautiously, was to be able to stay in her own shop at that hour again without feeling watched, unreal, and ashamed.
